problem: The chip "Tryptophan" sits under 'Limited evidence' with glycine and magnesium, so it reads as an over-the-counter supplement. In Canada, L-tryptophan above 220 mg/day is a prescription drug (Health Canada advisory, 30 May 2017; Pr Tryptan product monograph), and doses used for sleep are 1 to 5 g. The product monographs also warn of serotonin syndrome when it is combined with SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics or MAOIs. The same loop names an SSRI (escitalopram) two stops earlier, and the only safety text on the page is the generic "Supplements can interact with medicines, too." AASM 2017 also advises against L-tryptophan for insomnia.
fix: Relabel the chip "Tryptophan · prescription" and add a note: "In Canada, L-tryptophan at the doses studied for sleep is a prescription medicine. Don't combine it with antidepressants such as SSRIs unless a clinician advises it: together they can cause serotonin syndrome." Alternatively, remove the chip and keep "B6, folate and magnesium".

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/02-hpa-dysfunction.html line 163 (Longer-term stress step) and the 'Longer-term' curve
problem: "When stress goes on for months, some people's curves flatten: a smaller morning rise and a higher evening level." The 'smaller morning rise' part goes against the main meta-analysis of the awakening response (Chida & Steptoe, Biol Psychol 2009, 147 studies). It found the rise was LARGER with job stress and general life stress, and smaller only with fatigue, burnout or exhaustion. The pattern that is supported for chronic stress is a lower morning LEVEL, a higher afternoon and evening level, a flatter slope and often a higher daily total (Miller, Chen & Zhou, Psychol Bull 2007: a 'high, flat' profile, with output falling as time since the stressor's onset grows).
fix: Replace with: "When stress goes on for months, some people's curves flatten: morning cortisol runs lower and evening cortisol higher, so the day's total can end up higher than usual." Cite Miller 2007 alongside Adam 2017 in the step 6 sources.

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/03-measuring-cortisol.html line 154 (step 5 'When the curve flattens') and line 181 (toggle readout)
problem: "A smaller rise, little drop across the day and a lower total. In research, flatter curves are linked with chronic stress and poorer health on average." The readout also says "Flatter pattern: a smaller rise, little drop and a lower total." Tying a LOWER total to chronic stress contradicts Miller 2007, where chronic stress gives a high, flat profile with a higher daily output. It also contradicts this site's own chapter 02 (higher evening level) and the chapter 03 AUC chip ("Higher or lower total"). Adam 2017 notes that a flatter slope can come from a lower morning value or a higher evening value.
fix: Step 5: "A smaller rise and little drop across the day. Depending on the cause, the day's total can end up higher or lower. In research, flatter slopes are linked with chronic stress and poorer health on average." Readout: "Flatter pattern: a smaller rise, little drop, and a total that can be higher or lower."

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/06-cycle-stop-points.html lines 145 and 166 (ashwagandha notes at Stops 1 and 3)
problem: The only warning is "Ashwagandha has been linked to rare cases of liver injury." That statement is accurate: Health Canada's Summary Safety Review (Health Product InfoWatch, August 2026) found a possible link to liver injury that 'cannot be ruled out', with at least 16 serious cases. For a public audience, though, the page leaves out the standard cautions. The Health Canada NHP monograph says to ask a practitioner before use in pregnancy or breastfeeding and warns about drowsiness. NCCIH advises avoiding it in pregnancy and breastfeeding and in thyroid or autoimmune disease, and lists interactions with thyroid hormone, sedatives, immunosuppressants, and diabetes and blood-pressure medicines. The page also doesn't say what liver injury looks like.
fix: "Ashwagandha has been linked to rare cases of liver injury: stop it and seek care if you notice yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine or itching. Avoid it if you are pregnant or breastfeeding, and check with a clinician first if you have a thyroid or autoimmune condition or take thyroid, sedative, diabetes, blood-pressure or immune-suppressing medicines."

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/06-cycle-stop-points.html (Stop 5 note) and assets/js/glossary.js line 61 ('hormone therapy'), plus the 'progestogen' entry
problem: "Anyone with a uterus who takes estrogen also needs a progestogen to protect its lining." The glossary adds "Prescription estrogen, with a progestogen if you have a uterus". Both are overstated. The NAMS 2022 position statement says a progestogen is not required with low-dose vaginal estrogen, and conjugated estrogens/bazedoxifene (available in Canada) protects the endometrium without one. Menopause readers using vaginal estrogen for genitourinary symptoms could conclude they also need progesterone. The chip "Progesterone (if you have a uterus)" is also narrower than the options: any progestogen, or the TSEC.
fix: Stop 5 note: "Anyone with a uterus who takes systemic estrogen (pills, patches or gels) also needs protection for its lining, usually a progestogen such as micronized progesterone. Low-dose vaginal estrogen doesn't need one." Chip: "Progestogen, such as progesterone (if you have a uterus)". Glossary 'hormone therapy': "Prescription estrogen, used to treat menopause symptoms such as hot flashes and night sweats. If you have a uterus, systemic estrogen is paired with a progestogen or another way of protecting its lining."

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/01-dose-response.html line 173 (Cushing's note) and the adrenal insufficiency note in step 2
problem: "This is Cushing's syndrome, most often caused by long-term steroid medicines." This is correct, but a public reader on prednisone or a similar medicine may take it as a reason to stop. Stopping long-term glucocorticoids abruptly can cause adrenal insufficiency or adrenal crisis. The adrenal insufficiency note also doesn't say the condition can be life-threatening (Bornstein 2016).
fix: Cushing's note: "This is Cushing's syndrome, most often caused by long-term steroid medicines such as prednisone. Never stop a steroid medicine suddenly: talk to your prescriber, because stopping abruptly can cause cortisol deficiency. Cushing's is diagnosed with specific blood, urine or late-night saliva tests." Adrenal insufficiency note: add "Untreated, it can become life-threatening (adrenal crisis)."

problem: "High evening cortisol in turn makes sleep lighter and more broken." This is not supported as a direct effect of cortisol. Controlled infusions in healthy people show that cortisol INCREASES slow-wave (deep) sleep and reduces REM (Born et al., JCEM 1989; Born et al., Am J Physiol 1991; Bohlhalter et al., Neurobiol Aging 1997). The arousal in insomnia is tied to wider stress-system activation (CRH, sympathetic drive) rather than to cortisol itself (Vgontzas 2001). High-dose steroid medicines can cause insomnia, but that is a separate point.
fix: "In turn, an overactive stress system in the evening, as seen in chronic insomnia, goes with lighter, more broken sleep. The brain's stress signals seem to drive this more than cortisol itself."

problem: "A dark, cool (around 16–19 °C) and quiet bedroom". The 16–19 °C range has no evidence base, and the cited source (Okamoto-Mizuno 2012) gives no target. It finds that in real-life conditions heat hurts sleep, and it warns that cold affects cardiac autonomic responses. In older adults, the best sleep efficiency was at 20–25 °C (Baniassadi et al., Sci Total Environ 2023). WHO Housing and Health Guidelines (2018) recommend indoor temperatures of at least 18 °C in cold seasons, higher for vulnerable people. A 16 °C target falls below that minimum. The WHO 30 dB noise figure is fine.
fix: "A dark, quiet bedroom that feels comfortably cool, with bedding you can adjust (overheating disrupts sleep more than mild cool does). WHO guidance suggests keeping background noise to about 30 dB, roughly a whisper." If a number is wanted: "around 18–20 °C for many people; older adults may sleep best a little warmer."

problem: "enough magnesium, B12, vitamin D, iron and folate, ideally from food, with testing if a deficiency is suspected." For this audience this is inaccurate on two points. Canada's Dietary Guidelines advise ALL adults 51 and over to take a daily 400 IU (10 µg) vitamin D supplement, whatever their test results. Anyone who could become pregnant (which includes perimenopause) should take a daily multivitamin with 0.4 mg folic acid. Choosing Wisely Canada also advises against routine vitamin D testing in low-risk adults, so 'testing if a deficiency is suspected' shouldn't be the route for vitamin D.
fix: "Basics: hydration, fibre, and enough magnesium, B12, iron and folate, ideally from food, with testing if a deficiency is suspected. Vitamin D is the exception: Health Canada advises everyone over 50 to take a daily 400 IU supplement, and anyone who could become pregnant should take a multivitamin with 0.4 mg folic acid."

area: /Users/peterphua/Claude Code/hormone-explainers-public/06-cycle-stop-points.html line 155 (Stop 2 Rx chips), 08-pyramid-of-interventions.html line 151, assets/js/glossary.js line 27 ('metformin')
problem: Metformin and GLP-1 medicines appear as prescription treatments for 'insulin resistance', and the glossary says metformin is "A common prescription medicine for type 2 diabetes and insulin resistance." Neither is approved in Canada for insulin resistance as such. Metformin is approved for type 2 diabetes and used off-label in prediabetes and PCOS (Diabetes Canada; Teede 2023). GLP-1 receptor agonists are approved for type 2 diabetes and, for some agents, chronic weight management in people who meet BMI criteria (Wharton 2020). CHANGES-MEDICAL.md calls them 'correctly indicated', which overstates their approved use.
fix: Stop 2: add a note "Metformin is approved for type 2 diabetes and sometimes used for prediabetes or PCOS. GLP-1 medicines are approved for type 2 diabetes and, for some, weight management." Glossary: "A common prescription medicine for type 2 diabetes, also used for prediabetes and PCOS. It lowers the sugar the liver releases and helps the body respond better to insulin." Pyramid: "...then prescription medicines such as metformin or GLP-1 medicines if you have prediabetes, type 2 diabetes or obesity (discuss with a clinician)."

problem: "It declines from mid-life." This is wrong on timing. Slow-wave sleep falls most steeply between early adulthood and midlife (Van Cauter et al., JAMA 2000: 18.9% at age 16–25 vs 3.4% at 36–50 in men, with no further significant fall into late life; Ohayon 2004). Women keep more of it than men.
fix: "Slow-wave sleep: the deepest stage of non-REM sleep, important for feeling restored. It declines with age, starting in early adulthood."

problem: "CBD · early evidence" appears under a heading about partners 'being studied as ways to calm the stress response'. The study the change log cites (Zuardi 1993) found the opposite direction: 300–600 mg CBD blunted the normal morning fall in cortisol, so cortisol stayed higher than with placebo. The human CBD evidence concerns subjective anxiety in lab stress tests, not lowering cortisol. CBD can also raise liver enzymes and interacts with many medicines (CYP enzymes).
fix: Chip: "CBD · anxiety studies, no cortisol drop shown". Change-log source: replace Zuardi 1993 with an anxiety trial (for example Bergamaschi et al., Neuropsychopharmacology 2011), or state that Zuardi found cortisol was higher.

problem: "The moving dot is that effect travelling around the ring." The arrows are one-way, so the ring asserts Mood/cognition → Estrogen and Estrogen → Melatonin as causal steps. Neither is established: mood does not lower estrogen, and human evidence that estrogen drives melatonin is weak. Stop 6's foundations also list "Cool, dark bedroom" and "Exercise" as melatonin levers. Darkness is the lever; room temperature doesn't change melatonin, and exercise effects on melatonin are small and depend on timing.
fix: "The moving dot shows how a problem in one area can pass to the next. The order around the ring is a simplification: not every step is a direct cause of the next." In Stop 6, change "Cool, dark bedroom" to "Dark bedroom" and drop "Exercise", or move it to Limited evidence.

problem: "SSRI, such as escitalopram" sits under the stop "Mood, fatigue, cognition". SSRIs are indicated for depression and anxiety disorders, not for fatigue or cognition (CANMAT 2023), and they can themselves cause fatigue.
fix: Chip: "SSRI, such as escitalopram, for depression or anxiety".

problem: (a) "The most impactful changes sit at the bottom of the pyramid and the most marketed at the top." This is stated as fact, and so is the 'MOST IMPACTFUL' label on the base. No evidence ranks sleep above physical activity or diet; the ordering is a clinical framework. (b) "fine-tuning exercise and shifting effort to a diet or meal plan brings further benefit" is an absolute. (c) "The exercise you enjoy and will keep doing beats any specific type" goes against the Canadian 24-Hour Movement Guidelines (2020), which call for about 150 min/week of moderate-to-vigorous activity plus muscle-strengthening at least twice a week. Resistance training specifically matters for bone and muscle after menopause.
fix: (a) "In this framework, the foundations sit at the bottom and the most marketed options at the top." (b) "...can bring further benefit." (c) "The best exercise is the kind you'll keep doing. Over a week, aim for about 150 minutes of moderate activity plus muscle-strengthening at least twice."

problem: "Evening: cortisol low, melatonin high." In the evening melatonin is only starting to rise (dim-light melatonin onset is about 2 h before habitual sleep); it is high overnight and peaks in the small hours, as the landing page says. "Stressed evening: cortisol stays up and melatonin's rise can be blunted" implies that cortisol suppresses melatonin. CHANGES-MEDICAL.md itself says this is not established in humans; evening light is the documented suppressor (Gooley 2011).
fix: "Evening: cortisol near its low, melatonin starting to rise." and "Stressed evening: cortisol stays up, and sleep tends to suffer."

problem: "...then falls across the day to its low point around bedtime." The nadir falls around midnight, in the first hours of sleep, as the landing page says ("Cortisol bottoms out around midnight"). The two pages are inconsistent.
fix: "...then falls across the day, reaching its low point around midnight, early in the night's sleep."

problem: "A first sample taken 15 minutes late can miss the morning rise." The error is understated in one way and overstated in another. Stalder 2016 consensus guidelines require the first sample within about 5 minutes of waking. Delays of 5–15 minutes already distort the measured rise, first overestimating and then underestimating it, rather than 'missing' it.
fix: "Even a 5 to 15 minute delay in taking the first sample can make the morning rise look bigger or smaller than it really is."

problem: "↓ GnRH, ↓ growth hormone, central hypothyroidism". Cortisol excess reliably suppresses TSH and T4-to-T3 conversion, but overt central hypothyroidism is uncommon. For a public reader, the glossary term makes it sound like a standard feature.
fix: "↓ GnRH, ↓ growth hormone, ↓ TSH (which can lower thyroid hormone)"

problem: The HTML fallback caption still reads "Morning: cortisol rises sharply after waking while melatonin stays switched off." JavaScript replaces it with 'melatonin fades away', but crawlers, no-JS readers and link previews see the uncorrected text that CHANGES-MEDICAL.md says was fixed.
fix: Change the static text to match the script: "Morning: cortisol rises sharply after waking while melatonin fades away."

problem: "long fasts can raise cortisol, so they don't suit everyone." This is accurate (Bergendahl 1996), but it leaves out the real safety group. Fasting while taking insulin or sulfonylureas risks hypoglycemia, and people with a history of eating disorders or who are pregnant shouldn't fast. This matters because the same step goes on to name metformin and GLP-1 medicines.
fix: "...long fasts can raise cortisol, so they don't suit everyone. If you take diabetes medicines, are pregnant or have had an eating disorder, don't fast without medical advice."
